mainTopic: Teachings of רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי: God's prayer and anger, בלעם, משה's three requests, and God's good promises
overview: The amud starts with רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי, who proves from a פסוק that הקדוש ברוך הוא prays. His prayer is that His mercy should overcome His anger. A ברייתא tells how רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע blessed God with those same words, which teaches us never to take an ordinary person's ברכה lightly. The גמרא then teaches that you should not calm a person while he is angry, and it discusses God's daily moment of anger. That moment is so short that only בלעם could time it, and God held back His anger in בלעם's days to protect ישראל. The גמרא gives signs for that moment and tells how רבי יהושע בן לוי learned that it is wrong to curse people. Next come teachings about inner regret and about the three requests משה made. One of those requests leads to the famous question of why צדיקים suffer and רשעים prosper. The amud ends with משה seeing the knot of God's תפילין, and with proof that God never takes back a good promise, since משה's descendants grew to more than 600,000.

steps.title: God prays, learned from the words "My prayer"
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, in the name of רבי יוסי, proves from a פסוק in ישעיה that הקדוש ברוך הוא prays, because the פסוק says "My prayer" and not "their prayer."
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: How do we know that God prays? The פסוק says, "I will bring them to My holy mountain and make them joyful in the house of My prayer." It does not say "their prayer." It says "My prayer." So we learn that God prays.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a surprising teaching: God Himself prays. It proves this from one word in a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is about bringing the Jewish people to the בית המקדש, so we would expect it to call it "the house of their prayer." Instead it says "the house of My prayer." רבי יוסי reads that change as a hint that God has a prayer of His own.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? This asks for the source of an idea.
The Holy One, Blessed be He (God)
It does not say X, but rather Y. This points out the exact wording the פסוק chose.

steps.confusionAlert: This does not mean God needs something from someone above Him. The next steps show that His "prayer" is about His own wish to treat His children with mercy.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
From where do we know that the Holy One, Blessed be He, prays?
As it says: "I will bring them to My holy mountain,
phrases.notes: ישעיה 56:7

phrases.english: and make them joyful in the house of My prayer."
It does not say "their prayer,"
but rather "My prayer."
From here we learn that the Holy One, Blessed be He, prays.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: מִנַּיִן שֶׁהַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא מִתְפַּלֵּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new aggadic teaching.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: הקדוש ברוך הוא prays, as shown by the words "בית תפלתי" (the house of My prayer).

steps.title: What does God pray?
steps.stepSummary: Now that we know God prays, the גמרא asks what the words of His prayer are.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does He pray?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short follow-up question to set up the next step. It wants to know what God's prayer actually says.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 1 only proved that God prays. It did not say what He prays for. This question opens the way for רב's answer.

phrases.english: What does He pray?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי מְצַלֵּי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the content of the prayer proven in step 1.

steps.title: God's prayer: may My mercy overcome My anger
steps.stepSummary: רב זוטרא בר טוביה quotes רב: God prays that His mercy will overcome His anger, and that He will treat His children with mercy, going beyond the strict law.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זוטרא בר טוביה said in the name of רב: God prays, "May it be My will that My mercy overcome My anger, that My mercy rule over My other ways of acting, that I treat My children with mercy, and that I go beyond the strict law for them."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question. God's prayer is a wish that mercy will win over strict judgment when He deals with the Jewish people.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The prayer has four parts: mercy should beat anger, mercy should rule over His other traits, He should act with מדת רחמים, and He should go לפנים משורת הדין. All four say the same thing: God wants to treat His children kindly, even when strict judgment would call for punishment.

keyTerms.meaning: Beyond the strict line of the law

steps.whatToRemember: God's "prayer" is that His mercy should win over His anger and that He should treat His children beyond what strict justice requires.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַב זוּטְרָא בַּר טוֹבִיָּה, אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: Rav Zutra bar Toviyah said that Rav said:
"May it be My will
that My mercy overcome My anger,
and that My mercy prevail over My other attributes,
and that I act toward My children with the attribute of mercy,
and that I enter for them beyond the line of the law."
phrases.notes: Picture a judge stepping past the strict line of the law to be kinder than the rules require.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זוּטְרָא בַּר טוֹבִיָּה, אָמַר רַב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 2.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: God prays that His mercy will overcome His anger and that He will treat Israel with mercy, beyond the strict law.

steps.title: רבי ישמעאל blesses God in the קדש הקדשים
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא tells how רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע went in to offer קטורת and saw a vision of God, who asked him for a ברכה. He blessed God with the same words of mercy, and God nodded.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא teaches that רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע said: Once I went into the innermost room to offer incense. I saw אכתריאל יה ה' צבאות sitting on a high and lifted-up throne. He said to me, "ישמעאל, My son, bless Me!" I said to Him, "May it be Your will that Your mercy overcome Your anger, that Your mercy rule over Your other ways of acting, that You treat Your children with mercy, and that You go beyond the strict law for them." And He nodded His head to me.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a story from a ברייתא that matches רב's words almost exactly. A person blesses God with the very prayer that God prays, and God accepts it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברכה רבי ישמעאל gives is the same four-part prayer from step 3, changed from "My" to "Your." This backs up רב's teaching about what God's prayer is. God's nod shows He was pleased with the ברכה.

keyTerms.meaning: The innermost place, the קדש הקדשים

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אֱלִישָׁע:
phrases.english: It was taught in a baraita: Rabbi Yishmael ben Elisha said:
One time, I entered
to burn incense in the innermost place,
phrases.notes: "The innermost place" is the קדש הקדשים, the holiest room of the בית המקדש.

phrases.english: and I saw Akhteriel Yah, the Lord of Hosts,
phrases.notes: These are names of God.

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁהוּא יוֹשֵׁב עַל כִּסֵּא רָם וְנִשָּׂא,
phrases.english: sitting on a high and lifted-up throne.
And He said to me: "Yishmael, My son, bless Me!"
I said to Him: "May it be Your will
that Your mercy overcome Your anger,
and that Your mercy prevail over Your other attributes,
and that You act toward Your children with the attribute of mercy,
and that You enter for them beyond the line of the law."
And He nodded to me with His head.

steps.triggerLanguage: תַּנְיָא, אָמַר רַבִּי יִשְׁמָעֵאל בֶּן אֱלִישָׁע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a ברייתא that uses the same words as God's prayer in step 3.
steps.raayaObject: The wording of God's prayer given by רב.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא of רבי ישמעאל בן אלישע, who blessed God with these words and was answered with a nod.

steps.title: Never take an ordinary person's blessing lightly
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא draws the lesson from the story: if God asked a person for a ברכה and accepted it, we should value the ברכה of any ordinary person.
steps.simpleTranslation: This story teaches us that the ברכה of an ordinary person should not be light in your eyes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the story by telling us its practical lesson.
steps.deeperAnalysis: God asked a human being for a ברכה and nodded to accept it. So we should certainly respect a ברכה from any person, even a simple one.

keyTerms.meaning: The blessing of an ordinary (non-special) person

steps.whatToRemember: God Himself asked for and accepted a person's ברכה, so never treat anyone's ברכה as unimportant.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a well-known lesson in how to treat others: a ברכה from any person has real value.

phrases.english: And this teaches us
that the blessing of an ordinary person should not be
light in your eyes.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְקָא מַשְׁמַע לַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the practical lesson from the story in step 4.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Do not take lightly the ברכה of an ordinary person.

steps.title: Do not try to calm a person while he is angry
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, in the name of רבי יוסי, learns from a פסוק that you should not try to calm someone in the middle of his anger. Even הקדוש ברוך הוא told משה to wait until His anger passed.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן also said in the name of רבי יוסי: How do we know that you should not try to calm a person while he is angry? Because the פסוק says, 'My face will go, and I will give you rest.' God was telling משה: Wait for Me until My angry face passes, and then I will give you what you asked for.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching from the same pair of רבי יוחנן and רבי יוסי. It is about how to deal with a person who is angry.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן reads 'פני ילכו' as 'My face will pass,' meaning My angry face will go away. Only after that does God say 'והנחתי לך,' that He will grant משה's request. If God Himself waits for anger to pass before giving in, a person should also wait before trying to calm someone.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? This asks for a source.
Calming someone down, making peace with him
The angry face, the time of anger
And I will give you rest, meaning I will grant your request

steps.whyThisMatters: This is practical advice for real life. Making peace works best after the anger cools down, not in the middle of it.

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yochanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
From where do we know that we do not try to calm a person
at the time of his anger?
As it is written: 'My face will go, and I will give you rest.'
phrases.notes: שמות 33:14

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Moshe:
Wait for Me
until the face of anger passes,
and then I will grant you your request.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי: מִנַּיִן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching from the same רבי יוחנן and רבי יוסי pair as step 1. It continues the theme of how God's anger and mercy work.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: You should not try to calm a person in the middle of his anger. We learn this from God telling משה to wait until His anger passed.

steps.title: Can we really say God gets angry?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא questions the idea from step 6: does הקדוש ברוך הוא actually have anger?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is there really anger before the Holy One, Blessed be He?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא stops and questions a basic idea in the last step, that God has a 'face of anger.' This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 6 only works if God can be described as angry. The question 'ומי איכא' asks whether such a thing is possible. That challenges the reading of the פסוק at its root.

keyTerms.meaning: And is there really...? A doubting question

phrases.english: And is there really anger
before the Holy One, Blessed be He?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִי אִיכָּא רִתְחָא קַמֵּיהּ דְּקוּדְשָׁא בְּרִיךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the idea behind step 6 that God has a 'face of anger.'
steps.kashyaTarget: The idea in step 6 that God has anger that must pass
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: It seems hard to say that God feels anger. If He does not, the reading of 'פני ילכו' as an angry face falls apart.

steps.title: Yes, a ברייתא proves God has anger
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers yes, using a ברייתא that quotes the פסוק 'ואל זועם בכל יום.'
steps.simpleTranslation: Yes. As a ברייתא teaches: 'And God is angry every day.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a clear 'yes.' It proves this from a ברייתא that quotes a פסוק in תהלים.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק itself says 'אל זועם,' that God is angry. So speaking about God's anger comes straight from the פסוק. The reading in step 6 stands.

phrases.english: Yes, as it was taught in a ברייתא:
'And God is angry every day.'
phrases.notes: תהלים 7:12

steps.triggerLanguage: אִין, דְּתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 7.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Proof from a פסוק quoted in a ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might think anger cannot be said about God at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק says plainly that God is angry every day, so we may speak of God's anger.

steps.title: God's anger lasts only one tiny moment
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues: God's anger lasts only a רגע, which is 1/58,888 of an hour.
steps.simpleTranslation: How long does His anger last? A moment. And how long is a moment? One part out of 58,888 parts of an hour. That is a moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא keeps going. It explains that God's daily anger is extremely short and gives the exact length of that moment.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'אל זועם בכל יום' could sound like God is angry all day. The ברייתא says His anger lasts only a רגע, a tiny part of an hour. It then measures that רגע exactly, which prepares the next step about whether anyone could find that moment.

keyTerms.meaning: A moment, a very small unit of time

steps.confusionAlert: The ברייתא is not saying God is angry all day long. 'Every day' means there is a moment of anger each day, and it lasts only one רגע.

phrases.english: And how long does His anger last? A moment.
And how long is a moment?
One part out of fifty thousand and eight thousand
phrases.notes: רבוא means ten thousand, so 'five רבוא' is 50,000. Together the full number is 58,888.

phrases.english: and eight hundred and eighty-eight in an hour,
and that is a moment.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכַמָּה זַעְמוֹ — רֶגַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the same ברייתא and explains how long the anger from 'אל זועם בכל יום' lasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God's anger lasts only one רגע, which is 1/58,888 of an hour.

steps.title: Only בלעם could know the exact moment of God's anger
steps.stepSummary: No one can pinpoint that moment of anger except בלעם הרשע, because the פסוק says he 'knows the knowledge of the Most High.'
steps.simpleTranslation: No creature is able to pinpoint that exact time, except for בלעם הרשע, because the פסוק says about him: 'and he knows the knowledge of the Most High.'
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא ends by saying that nobody can figure out when that moment of anger happens. The one exception is בלעם הרשע, and it brings a פסוק as proof.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The moment is so short that no one can catch it. But the תורה says בלעם knew 'דעת עליון,' the knowledge of the Most High. The ברייתא reads that as knowing exactly when God's moment of anger comes.

keyTerms.meaning: To pinpoint exactly, to aim at the right time
Bilaam the wicked, the non-Jewish prophet who tried to curse ישראל
The knowledge of the Most High

steps.whatToRemember: God's anger lasts only one tiny moment each day, so short that no one can catch it except בלעם. And just as God waited for His anger to pass, we should wait for a person to calm down before trying to make peace.

phrases.english: And no creature is able
to pinpoint that exact time,
phrases.notes: 'That time' means the one רגע of God's anger from the last step.

phrases.english: except for Bilaam the wicked,
as it is written about him: 'and he knows the knowledge of the Most High.'
phrases.notes: במדבר 24:16

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵין כָּל בְּרִיָּה יְכוֹלָה לְכַוֵּין אוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the exact moment defined in step 9 and says who could know when it comes.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: No one can pinpoint God's moment of anger except בלעם, as the פסוק says he 'knows the knowledge of the Most High.'

steps.title: How could בלעם know God's mind if he did not understand his donkey?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the plain reading of 'he knows the knowledge of the Most High.' בלעם could not even understand his own donkey, so how could he know God's mind?
steps.simpleTranslation: Now, he did not even know the mind of his animal. Could he really have known the mind of the Most High?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the simple meaning of the פסוק quoted in step 10, which says בלעם 'knows the knowledge of the Most High.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the story of the donkey, בלעם did not understand why his donkey stopped, and the donkey had to rebuke him. Someone who misread his own animal surely could not understand God's mind. So the פסוק cannot mean that בלעם truly knew God's thoughts.

keyTerms.meaning: Now; used to begin a 'how can it be?' argument
The mind of his animal (בלעם's donkey)
The mind or knowledge of the Most High (God)

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא דַּעַת בְּהֶמְתּוֹ לֹא הֲוָה יָדַע,
phrases.english: Now, the mind of his animal he did not know;
phrases.notes: This points to the story of בלעם's talking donkey in במדבר 22, where he could not understand why the donkey stopped.

phrases.english: and the mind of the Most High he did know?
phrases.notes: This plays on the words of the פסוק from step 10, 'ויודע דעת עליון' (במדבר 24:16).

steps.triggerLanguage: הַשְׁתָּא דַּעַת בְּהֶמְתּוֹ לֹא הֲוָה יָדַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the plain meaning of the פסוק used in step 10
steps.kashyaTarget: The simple reading of 'ויודע דעת עליון', which suggests that בלעם truly knew God's mind
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A קל וחומר-style argument: if he could not understand a lowly animal, he certainly could not understand God.

steps.title: בלעם only knew how to pinpoint the moment of God's anger
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק does not mean that בלעם knew God's thoughts. It means he could pinpoint the exact moment when הקדוש ברוך הוא is angry.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the פסוק teaches that he knew how to aim for that exact moment when הקדוש ברוך הוא is angry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing what the פסוק means.
steps.deeperAnalysis: בלעם's 'knowledge' was not deep understanding of God. It was one specific skill: timing. He knew when that tiny moment of anger from step 9 would happen, so he could aim his curse at it.

keyTerms.meaning: To aim for or pinpoint exactly

phrases.english: Rather, it teaches that he knew
how to pinpoint that moment
in which the Holy One, Blessed be He, is angry.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, מְלַמֵּד שֶׁהָיָה יוֹדֵעַ לְכַוֵּין אוֹתָהּ שָׁעָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 11
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpretation of the פסוק in a narrower way
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The פסוק means that בלעם understood God's mind in general
steps.terutzMaskana: The פסוק means only that בלעם could time the exact moment of God's anger

steps.title: Support from the נביא: 'Remember what בלק advised'
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports this idea with a פסוק in מיכה, where the נביא tells ישראל to remember what בלק and בלעם planned.
steps.simpleTranslation: And this is what the נביא said to ישראל: 'My people, please remember what בלק king of מואב planned...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק that connects to the idea of בלעם trying to curse at the moment of anger. It is setting up the next move, where it explains this פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'והיינו' means 'this is what is meant by,' so the גמרא is linking the פסוק to what it just said. The connection only becomes clear in the next steps, where the end of the פסוק is explained.

keyTerms.meaning: And this is what is meant by; links a source to what was just said
And so on; the פסוק continues

phrases.english: And this is what the prophet said to Israel:
"My people, please remember
phrases.notes: מיכה 6:5

phrases.aramaic: מַה יָּעַץ בָּלָק מֶלֶךְ מוֹאָב וְגוֹ׳״.
phrases.english: what Balak king of Moab advised, etc."
phrases.notes: The part the גמרא is about to explain comes at the end of this פסוק: 'so that you may know the righteous acts of ה׳.'

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּאָמַר לְהוּ נָבִיא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a פסוק that supports the idea from step 12
steps.raayaObject: That בלעם tried to curse ישראל at the exact moment of God's anger

steps.title: What does 'to know the righteous acts of ה׳' mean?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the end of the פסוק means: 'so that you may know the righteous acts of ה׳.'
steps.simpleTranslation: What is meant by 'so that you may know the righteous acts of ה׳'?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the meaning of the last words of the פסוק. This sets up רבי אלעזר's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: It is not clear what 'righteous acts' have to do with the story of בלק and בלעם. Answering this question is what turns the פסוק into real support for step 12.

phrases.english: What is meant by "so that you may know the righteous acts of the Lord"?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לְמַעַן דַּעַת צִדְקוֹת ה׳
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks about the meaning of the end of the פסוק quoted in step 13
steps.sheelahInformationSought: What the 'righteous acts of ה׳' were in the story of בלק and בלעם

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: God's kindness was that He did not get angry in בלעם's days
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר explains that God's kindness was that He did not become angry at all while בלעם was around. If He had, ישראל would have been wiped out.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אלעזר said: הקדוש ברוך הוא said to ישראל, 'Know how many kindnesses I did for you. I did not get angry in the days of בלעם the wicked. If I had gotten angry, not a single survivor would have been left of the enemies of ישראל.'
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר answers the question: the 'righteous acts' are that God held back His anger the whole time בלעם was trying to curse ישראל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This completes the proof from the פסוק. בלעם's plan was to curse at the moment of anger, so God made sure there was no such moment during those days, and the curse could not work. 'Enemies of ישראל' is a polite way of saying ישראל themselves.

keyTerms.meaning: If it had been that; had I...
The enemies of ישראל; a polite way of saying ישראל themselves

steps.whatToRemember: בלעם's only 'knowledge' was timing God's moment of anger. God's great kindness was not becoming angry at all in בלעם's days, so his curses had nothing to work with.
steps.confusionAlert: 'The enemies of ישראל' here really means ישראל themselves. The גמרא avoids saying something bad about ישראל directly.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows why step 10 cared so much about God's moment of anger: in the story of בלעם, the survival of ישראל depended on it.

phrases.english: Rabbi Elazar said:

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל:
phrases.english: The Holy One, Blessed be He, said to Israel:
Know how many kindnesses I did for you
that I did not become angry in the days of Balaam the wicked,
for had I become angry,
there would not have remained of the enemies of Israel
phrases.notes: He really means ישראל themselves. It is a polite way to avoid saying ישראל would be destroyed.

phrases.english: a remnant or survivor.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר, אָמַר לָהֶם הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְיִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 14 and completes the proof begun in step 13
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The 'righteous acts' were God holding back His anger during בלעם's days, so that בלעם's curse could not take effect

steps.title: בלעם admits that God was not angry
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רבי אלעזר from בלעם's own words to בלק: he cannot curse or condemn when ה׳ has not done so.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what בלעם told בלק: 'How can I curse when God has not cursed, and how can I condemn when ה׳ has not condemned?' This teaches that all those days, God was not angry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to back up רבי אלעזר's point that God held back His anger while בלעם was around.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 15, רבי אלעזר said God did not get angry during that time. Here בלעם himself says he cannot condemn because ה׳ 'has not condemned' (לא זעם). The גמרא reads that word as 'was not angry,' which confirms רבי אלעזר.

keyTerms.meaning: I will condemn / be angry at

phrases.english: And this is what Bilam said to Balak:
"How can I curse whom God has not cursed,
phrases.notes: במדבר 23:8

phrases.english: and how can I condemn whom God has not condemned?"

phrases.aramaic: מְלַמֵּד שֶׁכָּל אוֹתָן הַיָּמִים לֹא זָעַם.
phrases.english: This teaches that all those days He was not angry.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְהַיְינוּ דְּקָאָמַר לֵיהּ בִּלְעָם לְבָלָק
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a פסוק to support רבי אלעזר's explanation in Step 15.
steps.raayaObject: רבי אלעזר's claim that God did not become angry during the days of בלעם.

steps.title: God's anger lasts only a moment
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how long God's anger lasts and answers right away: one רגע (a moment).
steps.simpleTranslation: How long does His anger last? A moment.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a quick question and answers it in the same breath: God's anger lasts only a רגע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains why בלעם needed to know the exact moment of God's anger. If the anger lasts only an instant, you would have to catch that precise second, which is what Step 12 said בלעם could do.

phrases.english: And how long is His anger?
A moment.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכַמָּה זַעְמוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the idea of God's anger and measures how long it lasts.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God's anger lasts only one moment (רגע).

steps.title: How long is a moment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how long a רגע actually is.
steps.simpleTranslation: And how long is a moment?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא now wants to measure the word רגע exactly. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying 'a moment' is vague. The גמרא wants a precise length of time, so we understand just how short God's anger is.

phrases.english: And how long is a moment?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְכַמָּה רֶגַע
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks to define the term רגע from Step 17.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The exact length of a רגע.

steps.title: A moment is as long as saying the word
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבין (some say רבי אבינא) says a רגע lasts as long as it takes to say the word itself.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבין, and some say רבי אבינא, said: a moment is as long as it takes to say it.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבין answers that a רגע lasts only as long as it takes to say the word 'רגע.'
steps.deeperAnalysis: This makes God's anger extremely short, just a split second. That is why only someone like בלעם, who could pinpoint that exact instant, could hope to use it.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי אָבִין וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי אֲבִינָא:
phrases.english: Rabbi Avin said, and some say Rabbi Avina:
A moment is like saying it.
phrases.notes: He means: as long as it takes to say the word רגע out loud.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי אָבִין וְאִיתֵּימָא רַבִּי אֲבִינָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 18.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A רגע is the time it takes to say the word רגע.

steps.title: Where do we learn that God's anger is only a moment?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for a source showing that God is angry for only a רגע.
steps.simpleTranslation: And from where do we know that He is angry for a moment?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for a פסוק to prove the claim that God's anger lasts only a moment. This sets up the proofs that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 17 stated the idea without a source. Now the גמרא wants to anchor it in a פסוק.

keyTerms.meaning: And from where do we know?

phrases.english: And from where do we know that He is angry for a moment?

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְנָא לָן דְּרֶגַע רָתַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the source of Step 17's statement.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: A פסוק showing that God's anger lasts only a moment.

steps.title: First proof from תהלים
steps.stepSummary: The פסוק in תהלים says God's anger is for a moment, but His favor is for a lifetime.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: 'For His anger is for a moment, life is in His favor.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק from תהלים that clearly says God's anger lasts a רגע.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The words 'רגע באפו' say outright that His anger is only a moment. The פסוק also contrasts this with His favor, which lasts a whole lifetime.

phrases.english: As it is said:
"For His anger is for a moment, life is in His favor."
phrases.notes: תהלים 30:6

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר כִּי רֶגַע בְּאַפּוֹ חַיִּים בִּרְצוֹנוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers Step 20 with a פסוק.
steps.raayaObject: That God's anger lasts only a moment.

steps.title: Second proof from ישעיהו
steps.stepSummary: Another option: the פסוק in ישעיהו says to hide for a brief moment until the anger passes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or if you want, learn it from here: 'Hide for a brief moment, until the anger passes.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא offers a second פסוק, from ישעיהו, as another source for the same idea.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This פסוק links the word רגע directly with the word זעם (anger). It tells us that if you hide for just a moment, the anger will already be over.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (another option)

phrases.english: And if you want, say it from here:
"Hide for a brief moment, until the anger passes."
phrases.notes: ישעיהו 26:20

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי בָּעֵית אֵימָא מֵהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, alternative source for the same point as Step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That God's anger lasts only a moment.
steps.raayaSupportSource: ישעיהו 26:20, 'חבי כמעט רגע עד יעבר זעם'.

steps.title: When is God angry?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks at what time this moment of anger happens.
steps.simpleTranslation: And when is He angry?
steps.whatsHappening: Now that we know how long the anger lasts, the גמרא asks when it happens. This sets up אביי's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question moves from 'how long' to 'when.' This connects back to the idea that בלעם knew the exact time of God's anger.

phrases.english: And when is He angry?

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאֵימַת רָתַח
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shifts from the length of the anger to its timing.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The time of day when God's anger happens.

steps.title: אביי: In the first three hours, shown by the rooster
steps.stepSummary: אביי says the anger comes in the first three hours of the day, at the moment the rooster's comb turns white and it stands on one leg.
steps.simpleTranslation: אביי said: during the first three hours of the day, when the rooster's comb turns white and it stands on one leg.
steps.whatsHappening: אביי answers when God is angry: during the first three hours of the day. The exact moment is shown by a sign in the rooster.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אביי gives both a general time window (the first three hours) and a sign for the precise instant. Since the anger lasts only a רגע, a sign is needed to catch the exact moment.
steps.whatToRemember: God's anger lasts only a רגע, the time it takes to say the word. It comes in the first three hours of the day, shown by the rooster's whitened comb as it stands on one leg. During בלעם's days, God held even this moment back to protect ישראל.

phrases.english: Abaye said:
During those first three hours,
when the comb of the rooster turns white
and it stands on one leg.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר אַבַּיֵי בְּהָנָךְ תְּלָת שָׁעֵי קַמָּיָיתָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 23.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The anger comes in the first three hours of the day, at the moment the rooster's comb turns white and it stands on one leg.

steps.title: The rooster stands on one leg all the time
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges אביי's sign: a rooster stands on one leg at every hour, so how can that mark the moment of anger?
steps.simpleTranslation: Doesn't the rooster stand this way every hour too?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is poking a hole in אביי's sign from the last step. Roosters stand on one leg all the time, so that cannot be a special signal.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sign only works if it shows up at one specific time. If the rooster stands on one leg every hour, that detail tells us nothing. The question is phrased as a question, but it works as a challenge to אביי.

phrases.english: Every single hour
it also stands this way?
phrases.notes: "It" means the rooster, standing on one leg as אביי described.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל שַׁעְתָּא וְשַׁעְתָּא נָמֵי קָאֵי הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the sign that אביי gave in step 24
steps.kashyaTarget: אביי's sign that the rooster stands on one leg
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A sign that happens all the time cannot mark one special moment

steps.title: The red streaks disappear at the moment of anger
steps.stepSummary: Usually the rooster's comb has red streaks. At the moment of anger the streaks are gone, and the comb is fully white.
steps.simpleTranslation: Every other hour there are red streaks in it. At that hour there are no red streaks in it.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. What makes the moment special is not the leg, but that the comb has no red streaks at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This explains the other half of אביי's sign: the comb turning white. Standing on one leg is common, but a comb with no red in it happens only at that moment. The two signs together point to the moment of anger.

phrases.english: Every other hour
there are red streaks in it,
phrases.notes: "It" is the rooster's comb, the red crest on its head.

phrases.english: at that hour
there are no red streaks in it.

steps.triggerLanguage: כֹּל שַׁעְתָּא אִית בֵּיהּ שׁוּרְיָיקֵי סוּמָּקֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 25
steps.terutzResolutionType: Points to a detail that sets this moment apart
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The sign is only that the rooster stands on one leg, which happens all the time
steps.terutzMaskana: The real sign is a comb with no red streaks at all, which happens only at the moment of anger

steps.title: רבי יהושע בן לוי waits for the moment to curse a מין
steps.stepSummary: A מין kept bothering רבי יהושע בן לוי with challenges from פסוקים. He watched a rooster so he could curse the man at the moment of anger, but he fell asleep right then.
steps.simpleTranslation: A certain heretic lived in the neighborhood of רבי יהושע בן לוי and kept bothering him a lot with פסוקים. One day he took a rooster, set it between the legs of the bed, and watched it. He thought: when that moment comes, I will curse him. When that moment came, he dozed off.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a story that puts the rooster sign into action. רבי יהושע בן לוי tried to use the moment of anger to curse someone, but he fell asleep at exactly that time.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The story shows the sign was taken seriously: a great אמורא actually used it. But he dozed off at the exact moment, and the story treats that as a message from Heaven. It sets up the lesson he draws in the next step.

phrases.english: A certain heretic

phrases.aramaic: דַּהֲוָה בְּשִׁבְבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי,
phrases.english: who lived in the neighborhood of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi,

phrases.aramaic: הֲוָה קָא מְצַעֵר לֵיהּ טוּבָא בִּקְרָאֵי.
phrases.english: would bother him a lot with verses.
One day he took a rooster,
and set it between the legs of the bed,
and watched it,
he thought: when that moment arrives,
I will curse him.
When that moment arrived, he dozed off.

steps.triggerLanguage: הַהוּא מִינָא דַּהֲוָה בְּשִׁבְבוּתֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tells a story where the rooster sign from steps 24-26 is put to use
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי יהושע בן לוי tried to curse the מין at the moment of anger but fell asleep at exactly that time

steps.title: Cursing people is not proper conduct
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי learns from falling asleep that it is not right to curse people, because God's mercy covers all His creations.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said: Learn from this that it is not proper conduct to do this. It is written: "His mercy is upon all His works."
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהושע בן לוי draws a lesson from falling asleep. Heaven was showing him that he should not curse the man, and he backs this up with a פסוק.
steps.deeperAnalysis: His sleep was not an accident; it stopped him from doing something improper. The פסוק teaches that God's mercy reaches everyone, even people who sin. So we should not try to bring harm on them, even a troublesome מין.

keyTerms.meaning: learn from this, conclude from this

steps.whatToRemember: Even though the moment of anger is real, a person should not use it to curse others. God's mercy is on all His creations.

phrases.english: He said: Learn from this,
it is not proper conduct to do this.
"His mercy is upon all His works" is written.
phrases.notes: תהלים 145:9

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר: שְׁמַע מִינַּהּ, לָאו אוֹרַח אַרְעָא לְמֶעְבַּד הָכִי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Draws the lesson from the story in step 27
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: It is not proper to curse people, because God's mercy covers all His creations

steps.title: A second פסוק: punishing is not good
steps.stepSummary: A second פסוק supports the lesson: even for a צדיק, causing someone to be punished is not good.
steps.simpleTranslation: And it is written: "Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds another פסוק to back up the lesson from the story.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first פסוק was about God's mercy for everyone. This פסוק adds that even a righteous person should not be the one who brings punishment on others. So רבי יהושע בן לוי, a צדיק, should not have tried to get the מין punished.

phrases.english: And it is written: "Punishment, even for the righteous, is not good."
phrases.notes: משלי 17:26. It is read here as saying that even for a צדיק, causing punishment is not good.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּכְתִיב: גַּם עָנוֹשׁ לַצַּדִּיק לֹא טוֹב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a second פסוק to support the lesson of step 28
steps.raayaObject: The lesson that one should not bring a curse or punishment on others

steps.title: Why God becomes angry at sunrise
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא in the name of רבי מאיר explains that God's daily anger comes at sunrise, when kings bow down to the sun.
steps.simpleTranslation: It was taught in the name of רבי מאיר: When the sun rises, all the kings of the East and the West put their crowns on their heads and bow down to the sun. Right away, הקדוש ברוך הוא becomes angry.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא has been talking about a moment each day when God is angry. Now it brings a ברייתא that explains what causes that anger.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now we knew that there is a daily moment of anger, but not why it happens. This ברייתא gives the reason. Every sunrise, the kings of the world bow to the sun as if it were a god, and that is what makes God angry.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ties the idea of God's anger to something real in the world, namely the worship of the sun, so the daily moment is no longer a mystery.

phrases.english: It was taught in the name of Rabbi Meir:
At the time when the sun rises,
and all the kings of the East and the West
place their crowns on their heads
and bow down to the sun,
immediately the Holy One, Blessed be He, becomes angry.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא, מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the cause of the daily moment of God's anger discussed in the previous steps.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: God becomes angry each day at sunrise because the kings bow down to the sun.

steps.title: One pang of regret beats many lashes
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי יוסי, teaches that one moment of real regret inside a person does more than many lashes.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: One pang of regret in a person's heart is better than many lashes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings another teaching from the same chain of sayings by רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי. This one is about how a person really changes.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Lashes are pain that comes from the outside. Regret is a feeling inside the person's own heart. רבי יוסי teaches that the inside feeling does more to change a person than many outside punishments.

keyTerms.meaning: Inner discipline, a pang of regret or self-rebuke

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:

phrases.aramaic: טוֹבָה מַרְדּוּת אַחַת בְּלִבּוֹ שֶׁל אָדָם
phrases.english: A single pang of regret in a person's heart is better
phrases.notes: מרדות literally means discipline; here it's the inner discipline of feeling regret.

phrases.english: than many lashes.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A new teaching in the series of statements by רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Inner regret is more effective than many outside punishments.

steps.title: Proof from the woman who returns to her first husband
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק in הושע shows a woman returning to her first husband because of her own regret.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it says: "And she will chase her lovers... and she will say, 'I will go and return to my first husband, for it was better for me then than now.'"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a פסוק to prove רבי יוסי's teaching about regret.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the פסוק, the woman stands for ישראל. What turns her back is her own thought: "it was better for me then than now." This shows that change that comes from inside the heart is what really brings a person back.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is said (introduces a פסוק)

phrases.english: as it is stated: "And she will chase her lovers, etc.
phrases.notes: הושע 2:9. וגו׳ means the פסוק continues and the גמרא skips ahead.

phrases.english: and she will say, 'I will go and return
to my first husband,
for it was better for me then than now.'"

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁנֶּאֱמַר: וְרִדְּפָה אֶת מְאַהֲבֶיהָ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supplies the scriptural source for רבי יוסי's teaching.
steps.raayaObject: That inner regret is what truly brings a person back.

steps.title: ריש לקיש: better than a hundred lashes
steps.stepSummary: ריש לקיש says regret is better than a full hundred lashes and brings a פסוק from משלי.
steps.simpleTranslation: ריש לקיש said: It is better than a hundred lashes, as it says: "A rebuke goes deeper into a wise person than a hundred blows to a fool."
steps.whatsHappening: ריש לקיש gives his own version of the same idea. He uses a different פסוק that names an exact number.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוסי said "many lashes" without a number. ריש לקיש says "a hundred," and his פסוק in משלי uses that number. A wise person is changed by words, while a fool is not changed even by a hundred blows.

phrases.english: And Reish Lakish said:
It is better than one hundred lashes,
as it is stated: "A rebuke goes deeper into a man of understanding
than striking a fool one hundred times."
phrases.notes: משלי 17:10

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרֵישׁ לָקִישׁ אָמַר, יוֹתֵר מִמֵּאָה מַלְקֻיוֹת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a parallel version of רבי יוסי's teaching, with a specific number and a different פסוק.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Inner regret is better than one hundred lashes.
steps.whatToRemember: Both רבי יוסי and ריש לקיש agree that real change comes from the inside. ריש לקיש says it is worth more than a hundred lashes.

steps.title: משה asked for three things and received them
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי יוסי, opens a new teaching: משה made three requests of God, and all were granted.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: משה asked for three things from הקדוש ברוך הוא, and He gave them to him.
steps.whatsHappening: This line sets up a list. The גמרא is about to go through משה's three requests one by one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is another teaching in the same chain from רבי יוחנן quoting רבי יוסי. The line only gives the headline, that there were three requests and all were granted. The details come in the next steps.

keyTerms.meaning: And He gave it to him, He granted it

phrases.aramaic: וְאָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן מִשּׁוּם רַבִּי יוֹסֵי:
phrases.english: And Rabbi Yoḥanan said in the name of Rabbi Yosei:
Moses requested three things

phrases.aramaic: מִלִּפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא, וְנָתַן לוֹ.
phrases.english: from the Holy One, Blessed be He, and He granted them to him.

steps.triggerLanguage: שְׁלֹשָׁה דְּבָרִים בִּקֵּשׁ מֹשֶׁה מִלִּפְנֵי הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new teaching in the same series of statements by רבי יוחנן in the name of רבי יוסי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה made three requests of God, and all three were granted.
steps.confusionAlert: This line only announces that there were three requests. The requests themselves come next: the first in step 35, the second in step 36, and the third in step 37.

steps.title: First request: the שכינה should rest on ישראל
steps.stepSummary: משה asked that the שכינה rest on ישראל, and the פסוק "Is it not in that You go with us" shows this.
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked that the שכינה rest on ישראל, and He granted it, as it says: "Is it not in that You go with us?"
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the first of משה's three requests and brings a פסוק as its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה's words "that You go with us" are read as a request for God's presence to stay with ישראל. The phrase "and He granted it" tells us God agreed.

phrases.english: He requested that the Divine Presence rest upon Israel,
and He granted it to him,
as it is stated: "Is it not in that You go with us?"
phrases.notes: שמות 33:16

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּקֵּשׁ שֶׁתִּשְׁרֶה שְׁכִינָה עַל יִשְׂרָאֵל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Fills in the first of the three requests announced in the previous step.
steps.raayaObject: משה's request that the שכינה rest on ישראל.

steps.title: Second request: the שכינה should not rest on the nations
steps.stepSummary: משה asked that the שכינה not rest on idol worshippers, and the words "so that we are set apart" show this.
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked that the שכינה not rest on idol worshippers, and He granted it, as it says: "So that we are set apart, I and Your people."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the second of משה's requests, again with a פסוק as its source.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first request was that the שכינה be with ישראל. This second request is that it be only with ישראל. The word "set apart" shows that משה wanted ישראל to be different from the other nations in this way.

keyTerms.meaning: Worshippers of stars, meaning idol worshippers or the nations
And we will be set apart, made distinct

phrases.english: He requested that the Divine Presence not rest
upon idol worshippers, and He granted it to him,
as it is stated: "So that we are set apart, I and Your people."
phrases.notes: This comes from the same פסוק as before, שמות 33:16, just a little further on.

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּקֵּשׁ שֶׁלֹּא תִּשְׁרֶה שְׁכִינָה עַל עוֹבְדֵי כּוֹכָבִים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the second of משה's three requests, which builds on the first.
steps.raayaObject: משה's request that the שכינה not rest on the nations.

steps.title: משה asked to know God's ways
steps.stepSummary: The third request: משה asked to understand how God runs the world. It was granted, as the פסוק shows.
steps.simpleTranslation: He asked to be shown the ways of the Holy One, Blessed be He, and God granted it, as it says: 'Show me, please, Your ways.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the third of משה's three requests and brings a פסוק to show it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Steps 35 and 36 brought the first two requests. This one is different: it is a request for understanding, not for the שכינה. It opens the famous question that comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: His ways, meaning how God runs the world
Please show me, let me know
And He granted it to him

phrases.aramaic: בִּקֵּשׁ לְהוֹדִיעוֹ דְּרָכָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא,
phrases.english: He asked to be shown the ways of the Holy One, Blessed be He,
phrases.notes: "He" is משה. This is the third of his three requests from step 34.

phrases.english: and He granted it to him,
as it is said: "Show me, please, Your ways,"
phrases.notes: שמות 33:13

steps.triggerLanguage: בִּקֵּשׁ לְהוֹדִיעוֹ דְּרָכָיו שֶׁל הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Third item in the list of three requests that began in step 34
steps.raayaObject: That משה asked to know God's ways and it was granted

steps.title: Why do good people suffer and bad people prosper?
steps.stepSummary: משה asks God why there are four kinds of people: a צדיק who does well, a צדיק who suffers, a רשע who does well, and a רשע who suffers.
steps.simpleTranslation: משה said: Master of the World! Why is there a righteous person who has good, a righteous person who has bad, a wicked person who has good, and a wicked person who has bad?
steps.whatsHappening: משה asks his question about God's ways. This sets up God's answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The question lists all four combinations of a person's deeds and what happens to him. Two of them seem unfair: a צדיק who suffers and a רשע who does well.

keyTerms.meaning: A righteous person whose life goes well
A righteous person whose life goes badly

phrases.english: He said before Him: Master of the World!

phrases.aramaic: מִפְּנֵי מָה יֵשׁ צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ,
phrases.english: Why is there a righteous person who has good,
and there is a righteous person who has bad,
there is a wicked person who has good,
and there is a wicked person who has bad?

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לְפָנָיו: רִבּוֹנוֹ שֶׁל עוֹלָם! מִפְּנֵי מָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Shows what "knowing God's ways" meant to משה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why righteous and wicked people sometimes get good and sometimes get bad

steps.title: God's answer: it depends on the parents
steps.stepSummary: God answers that a person's fate comes from his parent. A צדיק who does well is the son of a צדיק. A צדיק who suffers is the son of a רשע, and so on.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to him: משה, a righteous person who has good is a righteous son of a righteous father. A righteous person who has bad is a righteous son of a wicked father. A wicked person who has good is a wicked son of a righteous father. A wicked person who has bad is a wicked son of a wicked father.
steps.whatsHappening: God answers משה's question by pointing to each person's father.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this answer the person's own deeds are not enough to explain what happens to him. The father's deeds add reward or punishment. The גמרא will question this in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: A righteous person whose father was righteous
A righteous person whose father was wicked
A wicked person whose father was righteous

phrases.english: He said to him: Moshe,

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן צַדִּיק.
phrases.english: a righteous person who has good is a righteous person, son of a righteous person.

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: A righteous person who has bad is a righteous person, son of a wicked person.

phrases.aramaic: רָשָׁע וְטוֹב לוֹ — רָשָׁע בֶּן צַדִּיק.
phrases.english: A wicked person who has good is a wicked person, son of a righteous person.

phrases.aramaic: רָשָׁע וְרַע לוֹ — רָשָׁע בֶּן רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: A wicked person who has bad is a wicked person, son of a wicked person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר לוֹ: מֹשֶׁה, צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers משה's question
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A person's good or bad fortune comes from his father's righteousness or wickedness

steps.title: Are children really punished for their fathers?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes God's answer and questions it. Two פסוקים seem to clash: one says God remembers fathers' sins on children, and the other says children are not put to death for fathers.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Master said: A righteous person who has good is the son of a righteous person, and a righteous person who has bad is the son of a wicked person. Is that so? But it is written: 'He remembers the sin of fathers upon children,' and it is written: 'Children shall not be put to death for fathers,' and we set these verses against each other.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes God's answer to examine it. It starts a challenge by bringing up two פסוקים that it already knows contradict each other.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The problem is the idea that a צדיק suffers because of a wicked father. The two פסוקים raise the question of when children pay for their fathers' sins. The full force of the challenge comes in the next step, when the גמרא recalls how it resolved them.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that so? A sign of a challenge
He remembers the sin of fathers
And we set the verses against each other

phrases.english: The Master said:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is quoting God's answer from just above so it can look at it closely.

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן צַדִּיק,
phrases.english: a righteous person who has good is a righteous person, son of a righteous person,

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן רָשָׁע.
phrases.english: a righteous person who has bad is a righteous person, son of a wicked person.
Is that so?

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא כְּתִיב: ״פֹּקֵד עֲוֹן אָבוֹת עַל בָּנִים״,
phrases.english: But it is written: "He remembers the sin of fathers upon children,"
phrases.notes: שמות 34:7

phrases.english: and it is written: "and children shall not be put to death for fathers,"
phrases.notes: דברים 24:16

phrases.english: and we set the verses against each other,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר מָר: צַדִּיק וְטוֹב לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן צַדִּיק, צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ — צַדִּיק בֶּן רָשָׁע. אִינִּי?
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges God's answer from the previous step
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that a צדיק suffers because his father was a רשע
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The two פסוקים, as we already understand them, limit when children are punished for their fathers. The limit is spelled out in the next step.

steps.title: The known resolution makes the challenge sharper
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא recalls how it resolved the two פסוקים. Children are punished for their fathers' sins only when they continue doing those sins. A צדיק does not, so he should not suffer for his father.
steps.simpleTranslation: And we resolved it: It is not difficult. This verse is when they hold on to their fathers' deeds, and that verse is when they do not hold on to their fathers' deeds.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא recalls its earlier answer to the clash between the פסוקים. That answer finishes the challenge against God's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Children pay for their fathers' sins only if they keep those sins going. A צדיק, by definition, does not keep his father's wicked ways. So a צדיק בן רשע should not be punished, and the first answer cannot be right.

keyTerms.meaning: They hold on to their fathers' deeds, meaning they continue them

steps.confusionAlert: The words לא קשיא do not mean the challenge is over. They resolve the two פסוקים, and that very resolution is what proves God's first answer cannot mean what it seemed to mean.

phrases.english: and we resolved it: It is not difficult,
this one is when they hold their fathers' deeds in their hands,
phrases.notes: Holding the deeds "in their hands" means they keep doing the same sins their fathers did.

phrases.aramaic: הָא — כְּשֶׁאֵין אוֹחֲזִין מַעֲשֵׂה אֲבוֹתֵיהֶם בִּידֵיהֶם.
phrases.english: that one is when they do not hold their fathers' deeds in their hands.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמְשַׁנֵּינַן: לָא קַשְׁיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the challenge by recalling how the clash between the פסוקים was resolved
steps.kashyaTarget: God's answer that a צדיק בן רשע suffers because of his father
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Children are punished only when they continue their fathers' sins. A צדיק does not, so he cannot be suffering for his father.

steps.title: Rereading God's answer: complete or not complete
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rereads God's answer. It is not about the father at all. A completely righteous person does well, and a not-completely righteous person suffers. A not-completely wicked person does well, and a completely wicked person suffers.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, this is what He told him: A righteous person who has good is completely righteous. A righteous person who has bad is not completely righteous. A wicked person who has good is not completely wicked. A wicked person who has bad is completely wicked.
steps.whatsHappening: Since the first reading fell apart, the גמרא explains what God really meant.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The father's deeds are no longer the cause. Instead, what happens to a person depends on how complete his own righteousness or wickedness is. Some sins in a צדיק, or some good deeds in a רשע, explain why life seems mismatched.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather, this is what he meant to say to him
A righteous person who is not complete

steps.whatToRemember: God's answer to משה is finally read as being about the person himself. A צדיק who suffers is not completely righteous, and a רשע who prospers is not completely wicked. It is not about being punished for the father.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is a basic Jewish answer to why the righteous suffer. It keeps the rule that children are not punished for their fathers unless they continue their fathers' sins.

phrases.english: Rather, this is what He said to him:
a righteous person who has good is a completely righteous person,

phrases.aramaic: צַדִּיק וְרַע לוֹ — צַדִּיק שֶׁאֵינוֹ גָּמוּר,
phrases.english: a righteous person who has bad is a righteous person who is not complete,

phrases.aramaic: רָשָׁע וְטוֹב לוֹ — רָשָׁע שֶׁאֵינוֹ גָּמוּר,
phrases.english: a wicked person who has good is a wicked person who is not complete,
a wicked person who has bad is a completely wicked person.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא, הָכִי קָאָמַר לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by rereading God's answer
steps.terutzHavaAmina: God's answer seemed to mean that a person's fate depends on his father's deeds
steps.terutzMaskana: God's answer means that a person's fate depends on whether he is completely righteous or completely wicked

steps.title: רבי מאיר: Only two of משה's three requests were granted
steps.stepSummary: רבי מאיר disagrees with the view that משה got everything he asked for. Two requests were granted and one was not, because God is gracious and merciful even to people who are not worthy.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with רבי מאיר. רבי מאיר said: two requests were given to משה and one was not. As the פסוק says, 'I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious,' even if he is not worthy, and 'I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy,' even if he is not worthy.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells us that the view it just explained (that משה got all three requests) is argued on by רבי מאיר, who says one request was refused.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The refused request is the third one, from step 37, where משה asked to know God's ways. Step 38 shows that this meant understanding why good and bad things happen to people. רבי מאיר reads the פסוק to mean God gives grace and mercy even to people who do not deserve it, so God's way of choosing cannot be fully explained, and משה was not shown it.

keyTerms.meaning: And it disagrees: this view argues with another one

steps.confusionAlert: Step 42 explained God's answer about the four kinds of people. רבי מאיר is saying the opposite: משה was never given that answer at all.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with רבי מאיר,
for רבי מאיר said:
Two were given to him
and one was not given to him,
as it says: "And I will be gracious to whom I will be gracious"
phrases.notes: שמות 33:19

phrases.english: even though he is not worthy,
"and I will have mercy on whom I will have mercy"
even though he is not worthy.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְלִיגָא דְּרַבִּי מֵאִיר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Presents an opposing view: the explanation in Steps 39-42 assumed משה was given an answer, but רבי מאיר holds that he was not.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Only two of משה's requests were granted. God's way of giving grace and mercy, even to people who are not worthy, was not shown to him.

steps.title: You did not want to look then, so I do not want to show you now
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן קרחה explains why God told משה he could not see His face. משה refused to look when God wanted to show him, so now God refuses.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'And He said: You cannot see My face.' It was taught in the name of רבי יהושע בן קרחה: this is what God said to משה: 'When I wanted, you did not want. Now that you want, I do not want.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new פסוק and brings רבי יהושע בן קרחה's explanation of why משה was not allowed to see God's face.
steps.deeperAnalysis: משה hid his face at the burning bush. Here that is treated as a missed chance, and the refusal now is the result. This sets up the next step, where another אמורא sees the same act in a positive way.

phrases.english: "And He said: You cannot see My face"
phrases.notes: שמות 33:20

phrases.aramaic: תָּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה,
phrases.english: It was taught in the name of רבי יהושע בן קרחה:

phrases.aramaic: כָּךְ אָמַר לוֹ הַקָּדוֹשׁ בָּרוּךְ הוּא לְמֹשֶׁה:
phrases.english: This is what the Holy One, Blessed be He, said to משה:
When I wanted, you did not want;
phrases.notes: This means at the burning bush, when משה hid his face and would not look (שמות 3:6).

phrases.english: now that you want, I do not want.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּנָא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן קָרְחָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on to the next פסוק in the same conversation between God and משה.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה was not shown God's face because he turned away when God wanted to show it at the burning bush.

steps.title: רבי יונתן: Three acts earned משה three rewards
steps.stepSummary: רבי שמואל בר נחמני, quoting רבי יונתן, disagrees with רבי יהושע בן קרחה. In his view, משה's turning away at the bush earned him three rewards.
steps.simpleTranslation: This disagrees with what רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן. For רבי שמואל בר נחמני said in the name of רבי יונתן: as a reward for three things, משה earned three things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an opposing view and states its main rule. This line sets up the list of three rewards in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רבי יהושע בן קרחה, hiding his face was a fault that cost משה something. For רבי יונתן, it was a good act, done out of awe, and it was rewarded.

phrases.english: And this disagrees with רבי שמואל בר נחמני
who said in the name of רבי יונתן,
for רבי שמואל בר נחמני said
that רבי יונתן said:
As a reward for three things, he earned three things.

steps.triggerLanguage: וּפְלִיגָא דְּרַבִּי שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר נַחְמָנִי אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹנָתָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with Step 44 by treating משה's turning away as worthy of reward, not as a missed chance.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: משה's three acts of awe at the burning bush earned him three rewards.

steps.title: The three rewards, each matching what משה did
steps.stepSummary: Each phrase from the burning bush story is matched with a reward. Hiding his face earned him a glowing face. Being afraid made others afraid to come near him. Not looking earned him the right to see God's image.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because 'משה hid his face,' he earned a shining face. Because 'he was afraid,' he earned 'they were afraid to come near him.' Because he would not 'look,' he earned 'he sees the image of ה׳.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא lists the three rewards that רבי יונתן promised in the previous step. Each reward matches the act it came from.

steps.title: God never takes back a good promise
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן, quoting רבי יוסי, teaches that every good statement God makes is never taken back, even if it was said with a condition.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוחנן said in the name of רבי יוסי: every statement for good that came out of the mouth of the Holy One, Blessed be He, even if it was on a condition, He never took back.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new teaching about God's promises. Once God promises something good, it will happen, even if it was tied to a condition.
steps.deeperAnalysis: You might expect a conditional promise to fall away if the condition does not happen. רבי יוסי says that with a good promise from God, this never happens. The good always comes true in some form.

keyTerms.meaning: He did not take it back

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next steps, which prove the rule from God's promise to משה.

steps.title: The promise to make משה a mighty nation
steps.stepSummary: God promised to destroy the people and make a mighty nation from משה. משה's prayer canceled the decree, yet the promise still came true through his descendants.
steps.simpleTranslation: We know it from משה רבינו. God said: 'Leave Me alone, and I will destroy them, and I will make you into a mighty nation.' Even though משה prayed for mercy and the decree was canceled, God still fulfilled the promise through his descendants.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with God's promise to משה after the חטא העגל. The promise came true even though the plan it was tied to was canceled.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The promise to make משה a great nation was tied to destroying the people. Once משה's prayer canceled the destruction, you would think the promise was gone too. Instead, God kept the good part through משה's own descendants.

steps.title: 'Very many' means more than 600,000
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף teaches that 'very many' means more than 600,000. He learns this from the same word used about בני ישראל in מצרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף taught: 'very many' means more than 600,000. We learn this from the word for 'increasing' that appears in two places. Here it says 'were very many,' and there it says 'And the children of Israel were fruitful, swarmed, and multiplied.'
steps.whatsHappening: רב יוסף explains how big רחביה's family was. He compares it to the size of בני ישראל in מצרים, which was more than 600,000.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The same root word appears about רחביה's descendants and about בני ישראל in מצרים, so the גמרא learns one from the other with a גזירה שוה. Just as there it meant 600,000 and more, here too. So משה's descendants really became a nation as big as the people God had threatened to destroy, and the promise was fully kept.
